claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data in C. elegans and speculation about the implications for human embryo development.

claims.claim: In C. elegans zygotes, parental chromosomes are initially in separate pronuclei each surrounded by a nuclear envelope and meet for the first time during the first mitotic division.
claims.source: In the zygotes of humans, but also in Caenorhabditis elegans, parental chromosomes are initially in separate pronuclei each surrounded by a nuclear envelope (NE) and meet for the first time during the first mitotic division.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans and human embryo development.

claims.claim: The nuclear envelope of the pronuclei must be disassembled in a timely manner for proper mitosis to occur.
claims.source: For this mitosis to occur properly, the NE of the pronuclei must be disassembled in a timely manner (Rahman et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahman et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Nuclear envelope disassembly is essential to permit the mingling of the maternal and paternal chromosomes and their capture by the microtubules of the developing spindle.
claims.source: This step is essential to permit the mingling of the maternal and paternal chromosomes and their capture by the microtubules of the developing spindle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for nuclear envelope breakdown during mitosis.

claims.claim: After fertilization in C. elegans, the egg and sperm pronuclei meet near the posterior pole of the embryo.
claims.source: After fertilization, the egg and sperm pronuclei meet near the posterior pole of the embryo.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans embryo development.

claims.claim: After rotation and centration of the nucleo-centrosomal complex, the nuclear envelope breaks down in the vicinity of the centrosomes and between the juxtaposed pronuclei.
claims.source: After rotation and centration of the nucleo-centrosomal complex, the NE breaks down in the vicinity of the centrosomes and between the juxtaposed pronuclei.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans embryo development.

claims.claim: The breakdown of the envelope located between the two pronuclei starts with the formation of a membrane gap.
claims.source: The breakdown of the envelope located between the two pronuclei starts with the formation of a membrane gap (Audhya et al., 2007), most likely triggered by egg and sperm chromosomes that come into contact with the NE.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Audhya et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Gap formation depends on proper chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate.
claims.source: Accordingly, gap formation depends on proper chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate (Rahman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahman et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Complete disassembly of the nuclear envelope occurs at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition in C. elegans embryos.
claims.source: Complete disassembly of the NE occurs later at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition in C. elegans embryos (Lee et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2000.

claims.claim: If the nuclear envelope between the two pronuclei persists through anaphase, the two sets of parental chromosomes remain physically separated during the first mitosis.
claims.source: If the NE between the two pronuclei persists through anaphase, as is the case in mutant embryos with delays or defects in NEBD, the two sets of parental chromosomes remain physically separated during the first mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the physical barrier created by the persistent nuclear envelope.

claims.claim: When parental chromosomes remain separated during mitosis, the maternal and paternal chromosomes segregate into two separate DNA masses at each pole of the spindle, leading to the formation of two separate nuclei in each cell of the two cell embryo (paired nuclei phenotype).
claims.source: Consequently, the maternal and paternal chromosomes segregate into two separate DNA masses at each pole of the spindle. This in turn leads to the formation of two separate nuclei in each cell of the two cell embryo, called the 'paired nuclei' phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Rahman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahman et al., 2015 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Several studies have documented conditions that affect nuclear envelope breakdown and give rise to the paired nuclei phenotype.
claims.source: Several studies have documented conditions that affect NEBD and give rise to the paired nuclei phenotype (Audhya et al., 2007; Golden et al., 2009; Gorjánácz and Mattaj, 2009; Bahmanyar et al., 2014; Galy et al., 2008; Rahman et al., 2015; Martino et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The paired nuclei phenotype is typically associated with inactivation of the mitotic Polo-like kinase PLK-1.
claims.source: In particular, this phenotype is typically associated with inactivation of the mitotic Polo-like kinase (PLK-1 in C. elegans, Plk1 in humans and Polo in D. melanogaster) (Rahman et al., 2015; Martino et al., 2017), which regulates many aspects of mitotic entry and progression (Archambault and Glover, 2009; Zitouni et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Rahman et al., 2015 and Martino et al., 2017.

claims.claim: PLK-1 regulates many aspects of mitotic entry and progression.
claims.source: In particular, this phenotype is typically associated with inactivation of the mitotic Polo-like kinase (PLK-1 in C. elegans, Plk1 in humans and Polo in D. melanogaster) (Rahman et al., 2015; Martino et al., 2017), which regulates many aspects of mitotic entry and progression (Archambault and Glover, 2009; Zitouni et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Archambault and Glover, 2009 and Zitouni et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The critical targets of PLK-1 involved in nuclear envelope breakdown are largely unknown.
claims.source: However, the critical targets of PLK-1 involved in this process are largely unknown.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: PLK-1 is specifically recruited to the nuclear envelope in prophase just before nuclear envelope breakdown via its C-terminal Polo-Box domain in both human cells and C. elegans embryos.
claims.source: Consistent with a role in NEBD, PLK-1, is specifically recruited to the NE in prophase just before NEBD via its C-terminal Polo-Box domain (PBD), both in human cells (Linder et al., 2017) and in C. elegans embryos (Martino et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Linder et al., 2017 and Martino et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The PBD domain binds to specific phosphorylated sequence motifs (polo-docking sites) that are created by other priming kinases or are self-primed by PLK-1 itself.
claims.source: The PBD domain binds to specific phosphorylated sequence motifs (polo-docking sites) that are created by other priming kinases (non-self-priming) or are self-primed by PLK-1 itself, thus providing an efficient mechanism to regulate PLK-1 subcellular localization and substrate selectivity in space and time (Park et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2010.

claims.claim: At the nuclear envelope, PLK-1 could potentially regulate all the steps of nuclear envelope breakdown, in particular, depolymerization of the nuclear lamina.
claims.source: At the NE, PLK-1 could potentially regulate all the steps of NEBD, in particular, depolymerization of the nuclear lamina.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on PLK-1's localization and known functions.

claims.claim: The lamina is a rigid proteinaceous meshwork underlying the inner nuclear membrane, bridging the nuclear envelope and chromatin.
claims.source: The lamina is a rigid proteinaceous meshwork underlying the inner nuclear membrane, bridging the nuclear envelope and chromatin (Aaronson and Blobel, 1975; Goldman et al., 1986; Aebi et al., 1986; Burke and Stewart, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: All lamins are type V intermediate filaments composed of an unstructured N-terminal head, a central α-helical coiled-coil rod domain, and a C-terminal tail domain.
claims.source: All lamins are type V intermediate filaments composed of an unstructured N-terminal head, a central α-helical coiled-coil rod domain, and a C-terminal tail domain (Stuurman et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Stuurman et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Lamin filaments are composed of lamin dimers, which assemble into dimeric head-to-tail polymers that then assemble laterally into a protofilament with a uniform shape rod of around 3.5 nm in diameter.
claims.source: Lamin filaments are composed of lamin dimers, which assemble into dimeric head-to-tail polymers. Two head-to-tail polymers then assemble laterally into a protofilament with a uniform shape rod of around 3.5 nm in diameter (Turgay et al., 2017; Ahn et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Turgay et al., 2017 and Ahn et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Lamin filaments depolymerization is triggered by mitotic phosphorylation of the head and tail domains.
claims.source: Lamin filaments depolymerization is triggered by mitotic phosphorylation of the head and tail domains (Gerace and Blobel, 1980; Heald and McKeon, 1990; Mühlhäusser and Kutay, 2007) but the regulation of lamin phosphorylation is complex and not fully understood (Machowska et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The regulation of lamin phosphorylation is complex and not fully understood.
claims.source: Lamin filaments depolymerization is triggered by mitotic phosphorylation of the head and tail domains (Gerace and Blobel, 1980; Heald and McKeon, 1990; Mühlhäusser and Kutay, 2007) but the regulation of lamin phosphorylation is complex and not fully understood (Machowska et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge supported by citation to Machowska et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Conserved Cdk consensus motifs (S/T-P) are present in most lamins and their phosphorylation is important for lamina disassembly in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: Conserved Cdk (Cyclin-dependent kinase) consensus motifs (S/T-P) are present in most lamins and their phosphorylation is important for lamina disassembly in vitro and in vivo (Ward and Kirschner, 1990; Heald and McKeon, 1990; Peter et al., 1990; Peter et al., 1991; Dessev et al., 1991; Mehsen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In most studies conducted in vivo, the impact of lamin-phosphosite mutations on lamina disassembly during mitosis has been investigated only in the presence of endogenous phosphorylatable lamin.
claims.source: However, in most studies conducted in vivo, the impact of lamin-phosphosite mutations on lamina disassembly during mitosis has been investigated only in the presence of endogenous phosphorylatable lamin.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in previous studies.

claims.claim: Protein Kinase C (PKC) has been proposed to act in concert with Cdk1 to promote phosphorylation-dependent lamin B1 disassembly through lipid signaling in human cells.
claims.source: Based on a similar overexpression approach, Protein Kinase C (PKC) has been proposed to act in concert with Cdk1 to promote phosphorylation-dependent lamin B1 disassembly through lipid signaling in human cells (Mall et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Mall et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Multiple kinases cooperate to promote efficient mitotic lamin disassembly.
claims.source: These observations suggest that multiple kinases cooperate to promote efficient mitotic lamin disassembly.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple kinases can phosphorylate lamins.

claims.claim: The lamina persists during mitosis upon plk-1 inactivation, resulting in a paired nuclei phenotype.
claims.source: Although Plk1 has not been directly implicated in lamin phosphorylation during mitosis, the lamina persists during mitosis upon plk-1 inactivation, resulting in a paired nuclei phenotype, consistent with a possible role of PLK-1 in lamina depolymerization in C. elegans.
claims.evidence: This is an observation that suggests a role for PLK-1 in lamina depolymerization.

claims.claim: Partial inactivation of lmn-1 suppresses the paired nuclei phenotype of plk-1 temperature-sensitive mutant embryos.
claims.source: Moreover, partial inactivation of lmn-1, encoding the unique lamin isoform (B-type) expressed in C elegans (Liu et al., 2000), suppresses the paired nuclei phenotype of plk-1 temperature-sensitive (ts) mutant embryos (Rahman et al., 2015; Martino et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Rahman et al., 2015 and Martino et al., 2017.

claims.claim: C. elegans expresses a unique lamin isoform (B-type) encoded by lmn-1.
claims.source: Moreover, partial inactivation of lmn-1, encoding the unique lamin isoform (B-type) expressed in C elegans (Liu et al., 2000), suppresses the paired nuclei phenotype of plk-1 temperature-sensitive (ts) mutant embryos (Rahman et al., 2015; Martino et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Liu et al., 2000.

claims.claim: PLK-1 directly phosphorylates LMN-1 at multiple sites in the head and tail domains to trigger lamina depolymerization.
claims.source: Here we show that PLK-1 directly phosphorylates LMN-1 at multiple sites in the head and tail domains to trigger lamina depolymerization.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays and mass spectrometry analysis.

claims.claim: Expression of non-phosphorylatable versions of LMN-1 prevents lamina depolymerization during mitosis, which is sufficient to induce the formation of 2-cell embryos with a paired nuclei phenotype.
claims.source: Accordingly, the expression of non-phosphorylatable versions of LMN-1 prevents lamina depolymerization during mitosis, which is sufficient to induce the formation of 2cell embryos with a paired nuclei phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging experiments with lmn-1 8A mutant embryos.

claims.claim: PLK-1 reconstitutes the depolymerization of pre-assembled LMN-1 filaments in vitro.
claims.source: Furthermore, we reconstitute the depolymerization of pre-assembled LMN-1 filaments by PLK-1 in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro filament depolymerization assays and electron microscopy.

claims.claim: PLK-1 is a direct lamin kinase in C. elegans and possibly also in other organisms.
claims.source: Our findings demonstrate that PLK-1 is a direct lamin kinase in C. elegans and possibly also in other organisms.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data in C. elegans and speculation about conservation in other organisms.

claims.claim: PLK-1-mediated phosphorylation induced a mobility shift of the GST-LMN-1 head and tail fragments with the appearance of multiple bands on Phos-Tag SDS-PAGE.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1C, PLK-1-mediated phosphorylation induced a mobility shift of the GST-LMN-1 [H] and [T] fragments with the appearance of multiple bands on Phos-Tag SDS-PAGE, but not GST.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the Phos-Tag SDS-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Aurora A and Cyclin B-Cdk1 failed to induce a mobility shift of GST-LMN-1 head fragment.
claims.source: In a similar assay, the other mitotic kinases Aurora A and Cyclin B-Cdk1 failed to induce a mobility shift of GST-LMN-1 [H] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) indicating that PLK-1, but not these other mitotic kinases, phosphorylates LMN-1 in vitro, possibly at multiple residues.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 at at least 15 (S/T) residues distributed in the head and tail domains.
claims.source: We then subjected the LMN-1 head and tail fragments, phosphorylated in vitro by PLK-1, to mass spectrometry analysis and identified at least 15 (S/T) phosphorylated residues distributed in the head (S18, S21, S22, S24, S32, S35, T36, T40 and S41) and the tail domains just upstream the Ig-Fold domain (T390, T397, S398, S403, S405, S406) (Figure 1D and E and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis of PLK-1-phosphorylated LMN-1 fragments.

claims.claim: Most of the PLK-1 phosphorylation sites on LMN-1 match the consensus motif for Plk1 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Sequence analysis revealed that most of these sites match the consensus motif for Plk1 phosphorylation [L(Φ)-D/E/N/Q-X-pS/pT-L(Φ)] or [pS/pT-F] (Supplementary file 2; Santamaria et al., 2011; Kettenbach et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison to known Plk1 consensus motifs from the literature.

claims.claim: Different mutated versions of LMN-1 head and tail fragments with serine and threonine substitutions displayed significantly dampened phosphorylation by PLK-1.
claims.source: Different mutated versions of these LMN-1 [H] and [T1] fragments, with different serine and threonine substitutions, displayed a significantly dampened phosphorylation by PLK-1, indicating that these residues are indeed the major PLK-1 phosphorylation sites on the head and the tail domains of LMN-1 (Figure 1F and G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by radioactive kinase assays shown in Figure 1F and G.

claims.claim: Substitution of six serines and threonines in the LMN-1 tail fragment entirely prevented phosphorylation by PLK-1.
claims.source: In particular, substitution of the six serines and threonines in the tail fragment entirely prevented phosphorylation by PLK-1 (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 1 - Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the radioactive kinase assay shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: C. elegans LMN-1 and lamins in nematodes do not harbor any Cdk S/T-P motifs in the head or tail domains.
claims.source: Multiple protein sequence alignments between vertebrates, Drosophila and nematode lamins, revealed that C. elegans LMN-1, and more broadly lamins in nematodes, do not harbor any Cdk S/T-P motifs in the head or in the tail domains (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by protein sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Proline residues are strikingly absent in the head and tail domains of lamins from nematodes.
claims.source: Proline residues, highlighted in red in the protein sequence alignment presented in Figure 2A, are strikingly absent in the head and tail domains of lamins from nematodes, consistent with the observation that Cyclin B-Cdk1 failed to phosphorylate GST-LMN-1[H] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by protein sequence alignment and kinase assay data.

claims.claim: Several sites phosphorylated by PLK-1 on C. elegans LMN-1 are located in equivalent position to SP or TP sites phosphorylated by Cyclin-Cdk1 kinase on lamins from other species.
claims.source: Instead, several sites phosphorylated by PLK-1 on C. elegans LMN-1 are located in equivalent position to SP or TP sites phosphorylated by Cyclin-Cdk1 kinase on lamins from other species (S18, S35, T36, T390 Figure 2A, black arrows at bottom of alignment) suggesting that PLK-1 might be the main kinase in C. elegans phosphorylating LMN-1 to trigger lamina disassembly during mitosis and to promote pronuclear fusion.
claims.evidence: This is based on protein sequence alignment and suggests a functional equivalence between PLK-1 in C. elegans and Cdk1 in other species.

claims.claim: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 on putative polo-docking sites in the head and tail domains.
claims.source: Protein sequence analysis also revealed that PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 on putative polo-docking sites (Figure 2A), which match the consensus for self-priming sites, in the head (20-SSL-24, 34-STL-38) and in the tail domain (404-SSG-408) suggesting that PLK-1 might recruit itself to the lamin via a self-priming mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and suggests a self-priming mechanism.

claims.claim: The LMN-1 head domain, pre-phosphorylated by PLK-1, readily interacted with the PLK-1 PBD in a phospho-dependent manner.
claims.source: As shown in the Figure 2—figure supplement 1A (panels a, b), the LMN-1 head, but not the tail domain, pre-phosphorylated by PLK-1 readily interacted with the PLK-1-PBD (panel a), but not with a version of the PBD carrying mutated phospho-pincers (panel b), demonstrating that this interaction is phospho-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Far-Western ligand-binding assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 on two polo-docking sites in the head domain for self-priming and binding in vitro.
claims.source: The introduced alanine substitution in one or the other polo-docking site did not prevent binding (Figure 2B, panel b, lanes 6 and 8) but alanine substitution of both sites abrogated binding of LMN-1 to the PLK-1 PBD (lane 10). We conclude that PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 on two polo-docking sites in the head domain for self-priming and binding in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Far-Western ligand-binding assay with mutated LMN-1 fragments shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Vertebrate and Drosophila lamins contain putative polo-docking sites in the head domain.
claims.source: Protein sequence analysis suggested that Plk1/Polo might also interact with lamins from other species, as vertebrate and Drosophila lamins contain putative polo-docking sites in the head domain (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on protein sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: 12 out of 21 lamins from vertebrates and Drosophila harbor the canonical STP site in the head domain.
claims.source: Notably, 12 out of 21 lamins from vertebrates and Drosophila harbor the canonical STP site in the head domain (Figure 2A), which perfectly matches the consensus for non-self-priming and binding (Park et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on protein sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A and comparison to known consensus motifs.

claims.claim: A robust interaction between human or Drosophila lamin phosphorylated by Cyclin B-Cdk1 and the Plk1 PBD was observed by Far-Western ligand-binding assay.
claims.source: As shown in the Figure 2C and D, a robust interaction between human or Drosophila lamin phosphorylated by Cyclin B-Cdk1 and the Plk1 PBD was observed by the Far-Western ligand-binding assay (Figure 2C and D, panel b lane 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Far-Western ligand-binding assay shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: The interaction between Cyclin B-Cdk1-phosphorylated lamins and Plk1 PBD is phospho-dependent.
claims.source: This interaction is phospho-dependent because no binding was observed using a mutated version of the PBD that is unable to recognize phosphopeptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D, panels b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Far-Western ligand-binding assay with mutated PBD shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: The canonical non-self-priming STP and SSP polo-docking sites accounted for all the PBD binding activity to Drosophila and human lamins.
claims.source: The canonical non-self-priming STP and SSP polo-docking sites accounted for all the PBD binding activity as substitution of the threonine and serine to alanine abrogated binding under these conditions (Figure 2C and D, panel b lane 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Far-Western ligand-binding assay with mutated lamin fragments shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: Plk1 binds pre-phosphorylated head domains of lamins from several species via self and non-self-priming mechanisms.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that Plk1 binds pre-phosphorylated head domains of lamins from several species via self and non-self-priming mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Far-Western ligand-binding assay data.

claims.claim: Eight of the fifteen LMN-1 residues identified as being phosphorylated by PLK-1 in vitro have been previously shown to be phosphorylated in vivo in the C. elegans germline.
claims.source: Notably, among the fifteen LMN-1 residues identified as being phosphorylated by PLK-1 in vitro, eight have been previously shown to be phosphorylated in vivo in the C. elegans germline (S21, S22, S24, S32, S397, S398, S403, S405 (Supplementary file 2) and sites indicated by blue arrows in Figure 2A; Link et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Link et al., 2018.

claims.claim: LMN-1 serine 32 is phosphorylated in early embryos in a PLK-1-dependent manner.
claims.source: Accordingly, indirect immunofluorescence using a phosphospecific antibody directed against the phosphorylated serine 32 of LMN-1 revealed that this site is readily modified in early embryos in a PLK-1-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the germline, LMN-1 phosphorylation by CHK-2 and PLK-2 contributes to transient lamina disassembly, facilitating homologous chromosome movement during meiotic prophase.
claims.source: In the germline, LMN-1 phosphorylation by the master meiotic kinases CHK-2, and to a lesser extent PLK-2, contribute to transient lamina disassembly, facilitating homologous chromosome movement during meiotic prophase (Link et al., 2018) and for review (Zetka et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Link et al., 2018 and Zetka et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Lamina disassembly is delayed in embryos expressing GFP::LMN-1 8A in a lmn-1 null deletion strain.
claims.source: Indeed, lamina disassembly is delayed in embryos expressing a gfp::lmn-1 transgene encoding a LMN-1 version carrying these eight serine residues replaced by alanines ([LMN-1 8A], Figure 3) in a lmn-1 null deletion strain (Link et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Link et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: In embryos expressing GFP::LMN-1 WT, the lamina was normally depolymerized at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition and was almost undetectable at anaphase.
claims.source: In embryos expressing GFP::LMN-1 WT, the lamina was normally depolymerized at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition and was almost undetectable at anaphase (Figure 3C panels b-e, h-k, Figure 3—video 1), however, lamina dispersal was prevented upon plk-1 inactivation (Figure 3C, panels n-q, t-w, Figure 3—video 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by spinning disk confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Lamina dispersal was prevented upon plk-1 inactivation in embryos expressing GFP::LMN-1 WT.
claims.source: In embryos expressing GFP::LMN-1 WT, the lamina was normally depolymerized at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition and was almost undetectable at anaphase (Figure 3C panels b-e, h-k, Figure 3—video 1), however, lamina dispersal was prevented upon plk-1 inactivation (Figure 3C, panels n-q, t-w, Figure 3—video 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by spinning disk confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The amount of GFP::LMN-1 at the nuclear envelope remained elevated throughout mitosis upon plk-1 inactivation.
claims.source: Quantification of the GFP signal showed that the amount of GFP::LMN-1 at the NE remained elevated throughout mitosis upon plk-1 inactivation (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of GFP signal shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Lamina disassembly was significantly delayed in embryos expressing the gfp::lmn-1 8A transgene.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations (Link et al., 2018), lamina disassembly was also significantly delayed in embryos expressing the gfp::lmn-1 8A transgene (Figure 3—video 3) but this phenotype was greatly exacerbated upon plk-1 inactivation (Figure 3E, compare panels e-k with q-w, Figure 3—video 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by spinning disk confocal microscopy and is consistent with previous observations.

claims.claim: In gfp::lmn-1 8A mutant embryos, the lamina eventually disappeared in the vicinity of the centrosomes and between the parental chromosomes during anaphase, leading to two-cell embryos with a single nucleus in each blastomere.
claims.source: In gfp::lmn-1 8A mutant embryos, the lamina eventually disappeared in the vicinity of the centrosomes and between the parental chromosomes during anaphase (panels d-e, j-k) leading to two-cell embryos with a single nucleus in each blastomere at the two-cell stage (panels f-I, Figure 3—video 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by spinning disk confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Upon plk-1 inactivation in gfp::lmn-1 8A mutant embryos, a dense meshwork of GFP::LMN-1 8A filaments encased the chromosomes throughout mitosis, systematically resulting in the formation of embryos with a paired nuclei phenotype.
claims.source: By contrast, upon plk-1(RNAi), a dense meshwork of GFP::LMN-1 8A filaments encased the chromosomes throughout mitosis, systematically resulting in the formation of embryos with a paired nuclei phenotype (Figure 3E, panels r-x, Figure 3—video 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by spinning disk confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: GFP::LMN-1 8A levels at the nuclear envelope did not decrease during mitosis upon plk-1 inactivation as compared to control conditions.
claims.source: Quantification of the GFP signal confirmed that GFP::LMN-1 8A levels at the NE did not decrease during mitosis upon plk-1 inactivation as compared to control conditions (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of GFP signal shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 to promote complete lamina disassembly during mitosis in early C. elegans embryos.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 to promote complete lamina disassembly during mitosis in early C. elegans embryos.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that plk-1 inactivation prevents lamina disassembly and that this effect is exacerbated in lmn-1 8A mutants.

claims.claim: A small percentage of gfp::lmn-1 8A mutant embryos presented a double paired nuclei phenotype (8 out of 100).
claims.source: Supporting this latter hypothesis, we noticed that a small percentage of gfp::lmn-1 8A mutant embryos presented a double paired nuclei phenotype (8 out of 100, n = 100).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: The GFP tag in the N-terminal part of LMN-1 might destabilize the lamina filaments that assemble longitudinally in a head-to-tail fashion.
claims.source: We reasoned that the GFP tag in the N-terminal part of LMN-1 might destabilize the lamina filaments that assemble longitudinally in a head-to-tail fashion.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the structure of lamin filaments and the position of the GFP tag.

claims.claim: More than 65% of lmn-1 8A mutant embryos presented a penetrant paired nuclei phenotype at the two-cell stage.
claims.source: Remarkably, time-lapse differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy showed that more than 65% of lmn-1 8A mutant embryos presented a penetrant paired nuclei phenotype at the two-cell stage (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by DIC microscopy shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Almost 25% of lmn-1 8A mutant embryos died.
claims.source: Furthermore, almost 25% of these embryos died (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1) illustrating the functional importance of depolymerizing the lamina in mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by embryonic viability assay shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: LMN-1 immunostaining confirmed the persistence of the lamina between the parental chromosomes during mitosis in lmn-1 8A mutant embryos.
claims.source: LMN-1 immunostaining confirmed the persistence of the lamina between the parental chromosomes during mitosis in lmn-1 8A mutant embryos (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: In wild-type embryos, the lamina disappears first in the vicinity of the centrosomes in pro-metaphase and from between the chromosomes during metaphase, and is undetectable by anaphase.

results.result: PLK-1 directly phosphorylates LMN-1 at multiple sites in vitro. Mass spectrometry identified at least 15 phosphorylated residues in the head and tail domains, most matching PLK-1 consensus motifs. Mutational analysis confirmed these sites as major PLK-1 phosphorylation targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C43 provide converging evidence from in vitro kinase assays (C38), specificity controls showing Aurora A and Cyclin B-Cdk1 do not phosphorylate LMN-1 (C39), mass spectrometry identification of 15 sites (C40), consensus motif matching (C41), and mutational validation (C42-C43). The data are internally consistent and use appropriate biochemical methods.

results.result: C. elegans LMN-1 lacks Cdk consensus motifs (S/T-P) in head and tail domains, but several PLK-1 phosphorylation sites are positioned equivalently to Cdk sites in other species' lamins. This suggests PLK-1 may functionally replace Cdk1 in C. elegans lamina regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by protein sequence alignment data showing absence of proline residues in nematode lamins (C44-C45) and positional equivalence of PLK-1 sites to Cdk sites in other species (C46). The inference about functional replacement is reasonable but remains speculative without direct functional comparison.

results.result: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 on two polo-docking sites in the head domain, enabling self-priming and PBD binding. Far-Western assays demonstrate phospho-dependent interaction between PLK-1-phosphorylated LMN-1 head domain and PLK-1 PBD.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by sequence analysis identifying putative polo-docking sites (C47), Far-Western assays showing phospho-dependent PBD binding (C48), and mutational analysis demonstrating both sites are required for binding (C49). The self-priming mechanism is well-documented for PLK-1.

results.result: Plk1 binds pre-phosphorylated head domains of lamins from multiple species (Drosophila, human) via non-self-priming mechanisms. Cyclin B-Cdk1 phosphorylation creates polo-docking sites that enable phospho-dependent Plk1 PBD binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are supported by sequence analysis showing canonical polo-docking sites in vertebrate and Drosophila lamins (C50-C51), Far-Western assays demonstrating Cdk1-phosphorylation-dependent PBD binding (C52-C53), and mutational validation (C54). This establishes conservation of the mechanism across species.

results.result: Eight of fifteen PLK-1 phosphorylation sites identified in vitro are phosphorylated in vivo in C. elegans germline and early embryos. These sites contribute to lamina disassembly during both meiosis and mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by prior work (Link et al., 2018) showing in vivo phosphorylation (C56), phospho-specific antibody validation (C57), functional roles in germline (C58), and delayed lamina disassembly in 8A mutants (C59). The connection between in vitro and in vivo phosphorylation strengthens the physiological relevance.

results.result: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 to promote complete lamina disassembly during mitosis in early C. elegans embryos. plk-1 inactivation prevents lamina dispersal in wild-type embryos, and this effect is exacerbated in lmn-1 8A mutants where GFP::LMN-1 8A persists throughout mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are supported by quantitative live imaging showing normal lamina depolymerization in wild-type (C60), prevention upon plk-1 inactivation (C61-C62), delayed disassembly in 8A mutants (C63-C64), and complete stabilization when both conditions are combined (C65-C66). The genetic interaction strongly supports the conclusion (C67).

results.result: Untagged lmn-1 8A mutant embryos exhibit a penetrant paired nuclei phenotype (>65%) with ~25% embryonic lethality. Immunostaining confirms persistent lamina between parental chromosomes throughout mitosis, demonstrating that preventing LMN-1 phosphorylation is sufficient to cause chromosome separation defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C75 are supported by DIC microscopy showing high penetrance of paired nuclei (C70), viability assays demonstrating lethality (C71), and immunofluorescence confirming lamina persistence (C72-C74). The comparison between GFP-tagged (C68) and untagged versions addresses potential artifacts. The conclusion (C75) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: PLK-1::sGFP spatiotemporal localization during mitosis closely follows the timing and location of lamina depolymerization. PLK-1 is enriched where lamina first depolymerizes (centrosomes, between pronuclei) and absent where lamina persists.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by live imaging showing PLK-1 localization patterns (C76-C78) that correlate with lamina depolymerization dynamics. The correlation is strong, though the inference that this proves PLK-1 directly causes depolymerization (C79) requires the supporting biochemical data from other results.

results.result: PLK-1 phosphorylation promotes LMN-1 filament disassembly in vitro. Purified LMN-1 assembles into filaments that pellet upon centrifugation, but PLK-1 treatment causes release into supernatant and loss of filament structures visible by electron microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by electron microscopy confirming filament assembly (C80), pelleting assays showing PLK-1-dependent solubilization (C81), gel shift suggesting phosphorylation (C82), and EM showing filament loss (C83). This in vitro reconstitution directly demonstrates PLK-1's biochemical activity on lamins (C84).

results.result: Non-phosphorylatable LMN-1 8A is sufficient to physically separate parental chromosomes during the first zygotic mitosis. Photoconversion experiments show that in lmn-1 8A mutants, maternal and paternal chromosomes remain separated, with each paired nucleus receiving only one parental genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by photoconversion experiments directly tracking parental chromosomes (C85-C86). The conclusion that non-phosphorylatable LMN-1 is sufficient for separation (C87) and that PLK-1 promotes genome merging (C88) logically follows from the data. This is a key functional demonstration.

results.result: PLK-1-mediated lamina depolymerization is a prerequisite for membrane gap formation between pronuclei. In wild-type embryos, membrane scission coincides with chromosome alignment, but this event never occurs in lmn-1 8A mutants despite proper chromosome alignment in most embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 are supported by live imaging showing membrane scission in wild-type (C91), its absence in lmn-1 8A mutants (C93), and proper chromosome alignment in 7/12 mutant embryos (C93). This demonstrates that lamina depolymerization is required for membrane gap formation independent of chromosome alignment, supporting the conclusion (C95).

results.result: PLK-1 triggers lamina depolymerization in mitosis, which is essential for merging parental chromosomes into a single nucleus. Expression of LMN-1 with eight phosphosite mutations prevents membrane scission and chromosome merging, demonstrating that lamina depolymerization is a key step in this process.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C112 synthesize the major findings: PLK-1-dependent lamina depolymerization (C99), sufficiency of 8A mutations to prevent merging (C100, C110), and the requirement for membrane gap formation (C111-C112). The conclusion that lamina depolymerization is a key step (C101, C109, C112) is well-supported by the collective data.

results.result: Mutation of eight PLK-1 phosphorylation sites stabilizes the lamina but does not fully recapitulate plk-1 depletion effects. This suggests either the seven remaining sites contribute or PLK-1 phosphorylates other lamin-binding proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 acknowledge limitations in the 8A mutant analysis. The observation that 8A doesn't fully phenocopy plk-1 depletion (C115) is supported by the data. The speculation about additional sites or substrates (C116) is reasonable but requires further investigation.

results.result: N-terminal GFP tagging of LMN-1 appears to alter lamina assembly properties. The phenotype of GFP::LMN-1 8A is less severe than untagged LMN-1 8A, suggesting the tag may destabilize filaments.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 are supported by comparison of GFP-tagged (8% paired nuclei) versus untagged (67% paired nuclei) lmn-1 8A phenotypes. This is an important methodological observation about potential artifacts from fluorescent protein tags on structural proteins.

results.result: Lamina depolymerization in C. elegans is independent of Cyclin-Cdk and driven by PLK-1. In Drosophila, both CDK1 and Polo may contribute, as suggested by PLK-1 binding to Drosophila lamin Dm0 and prior work showing Polo is required for NEBD.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 are supported by the absence of Cdk sites in C. elegans LMN-1 (C44-C45), failure of Cdk1 to phosphorylate LMN-1 (C39), PLK-1 binding to Drosophila lamin (C130), and cited work on Polo's role in NEBD (C131-C132). The speculation about cooperative roles (C133) is reasonable but requires direct testing.

results.result: Plk1 could assist lamin A/C dispersal in human cells, as lamin A/C is phosphorylated on a polo-docking site during mitosis. This suggests potential conservation of PLK-1's role in lamina regulation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 are speculative (C134) but based on documented phosphorylation of human lamin A/C on polo-docking sites (C135). While the phosphorylation is established, the functional significance for Plk1-mediated lamina dispersal in human cells remains untested. This requires experimental validation.

results.result: A PLK-1-dependent lamina depolymerization process is essential for parental chromosome mixing in C. elegans. Given similarities between C. elegans and human embryo development, timely lamina depolymerization might be required in human embryos, and defects could cause genomic heterogeneity or multinucleated blastomeres.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 is well-supported by the C. elegans data. However, claims C137-C140 about human embryos are speculative, based on assumed similarities in spindle organization (C96-C98). While the speculation is reasonable given that human embryos also have centrosomal first divisions, direct evidence in human embryos is lacking.

results.result: PLK-1 phosphorylates LMN-1 to promote timely lamina disassembly and parental genome merging in C. elegans zygotes. Expression of non-phosphorylatable LMN-1 prevents chromosome mixing, and PLK-1 directly phosphorylates and depolymerizes LMN-1 in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from in vitro biochemistry (C3), in vivo genetics (C2), and functional assays. These are well-supported by the detailed experimental evidence in other result groups. The speculation about human relevance (C4) is acknowledged as such.

results.result: Background on C. elegans embryo development and nuclear envelope breakdown. Parental chromosomes are in separate pronuclei that must be disassembled for proper mitosis. PLK-1 is recruited to the nuclear envelope and regulates NEBD, but its critical targets were largely unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C21 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims set up the biological context and rationale for the study. The statement that PLK-1 targets were largely unknown (C18) justifies the research question.

results.result: Background on lamina structure and regulation. The lamina is a meshwork of type V intermediate filaments whose depolymerization is triggered by mitotic phosphorylation. Multiple kinases, including Cdk and PKC, have been implicated in lamina disassembly, but regulation is complex and not fully understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C30 provide established background on lamina biology supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the complexity of lamina regulation and the known roles of various kinases, setting up the rationale for investigating PLK-1's role.

results.result: Prior observations suggest PLK-1 role in lamina depolymerization in C. elegans. The lamina persists upon plk-1 inactivation, and partial lmn-1 inactivation suppresses the plk-1 mutant paired nuclei phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 cite prior work establishing genetic interactions between plk-1 and lmn-1. These observations provided the rationale for investigating whether LMN-1 is a direct PLK-1 substrate, which is the focus of the current study.

results.result: Background on membrane gap formation. Merging of parental chromosomes starts with membrane gap formation between pronuclei during chromosome alignment. This gap is absent in plk-1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 cite established knowledge about membrane gap formation from prior work. This provides context for understanding how lamina depolymerization relates to membrane remodeling during pronuclear fusion.

results.result: Comparison of embryo development across species. C. elegans and humans have centrosomal first divisions where parental chromosomes must align on a single spindle, unlike mouse where the first division is acentrosomal with separate spindles.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 cite established differences in early embryo development between species. This comparison supports the relevance of C. elegans findings to human biology and explains why the mechanism might differ in mouse.

results.result: Background on pronuclear membrane structure and fusion. Each pronucleus is surrounded by a double membrane with nuclear pores and lamina. Recent work showed membranes fuse via outer-outer and three-way junctions, with three-way junctions absent in plk-1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C108 cite recent work (Rahman et al., 2020) on pronuclear membrane fusion mechanisms. This provides context for discussing whether PLK-1 directly promotes membrane fusion versus enabling it through lamina depolymerization.

results.result: Embryonic lethality in lmn-1 8A mutants illustrates functional importance of lamina depolymerization. A similar defect in humans might cause drastic consequences including loss of heterozygosity.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by the viability data showing ~25% lethality. Claim C114 is speculation about human implications. The lethality demonstrates functional importance, though the specific causes of death are not determined.

results.result: Background on lamina depolymerization timing and kinase involvement across species. In human cells, lamina depolymerization occurs in prophase/pro-metaphase via Cyclin B-Cdk1. In Drosophila and C. elegans, depolymerization occurs at metaphase-to-anaphase transition when Cdk1 activity drops, suggesting other kinases are involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C127 cite established knowledge about species differences in lamina depolymerization timing and kinase involvement. This provides important context for why PLK-1 might be the primary kinase in C. elegans rather than Cdk1.
